comp_013:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for our annual penetration test by scoping the engagement and assembling a shortlist of candidate pen-test firms — but the final vendor choice must remain with me. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: our primary domain(s) and application/API endpoints in scope, cloud infrastructure providers used, whether this is for SOC 2 (or another framework) so we know required test types (network, web app, API, cloud config, social engineering, etc.), last year's pen test firm and report (if any), and our target testing window/deadline.
2. Draft a scope document listing: in-scope assets, out-of-scope items, test types needed, estimated environment size (hosts, endpoints, user roles), and desired timing.
3. Research and compile a comparison of 4-6 reputable, established pen-testing firms with relevant industry certifications (e.g., OSCP-certified testers, CREST accreditation) and SOC 2-familiar reporting formats. For each, note: specialties, typical turnaround, sample report quality if available, and how to request a quote.
4. Draft outreach emails or RFP requests to send to these firms, including our scope summary, so I can quickly request quotes.
5. Build a simple comparison table (firm, certifications, price range once quotes arrive, turnaround time, references) to help me weigh the options.

Done looks like: a finished scope document, a shortlist of vetted firms with comparison data, and ready-to-send outreach drafts — all organized in one summary for my review. Do not contact firms on my behalf, negotiate pricing, or select a vendor; selecting the firm involves weighing relationship and reputational factors only I can judge, so stop for human sign-off once the shortlist and outreach drafts are ready. Report back with the scope document, the firm comparison table, and the draft outreach messages for my review and final decision.

comp_013:n2.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but NOT sign) the Rules of Engagement (ROE) authorization for our annual penetration test. This document legally defines what the testing firm may attack, so only an authorized signer at my company can grant that permission — signing remains a human step.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for: the pen testing firm's name and contact, the agreed testing window (start/end dates), the in-scope assets (domains, IP ranges, applications, APIs), explicitly out-of-scope assets, allowed testing types (e.g., network, web app, social engineering, physical), any blackout windows or rate-limiting requirements, escalation/emergency contacts on both sides, and the name/title of our authorized signer.
2. If the testing firm has already sent a draft ROE or contract, ask me to share it so you can review it against the details above and flag any gaps, ambiguous scope language, missing contacts, or liability terms worth raising before signing.
3. Draft a clean summary of the ROE terms (scope, dates, contacts, authorized methods, exclusions) formatted for easy review, and prepare a checklist of open questions or discrepancies for me to resolve with the testing firm.
4. Note where the signature and date belong, and confirm who the authorized signer is per our internal policy.
5. Do NOT sign, e-sign, approve, accept terms, or submit the ROE on my behalf under any circumstances.

When your prep is complete, report back with: the finalized summary of scope/dates/contacts, the list of open questions or flagged risks, and confirmation of who needs to sign. Then explicitly stop for human sign-off — I or another authorized signer will review and execute the ROE ourselves.

comp_013:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the isolated test environment and accounts for our annual penetration test. Goal: have a fully provisioned, scoped-down environment and a set of least-privilege test accounts ready to hand to the pen test firm, with everything documented for the SOC 2 auditor trail.

Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have access to: (1) my company domain, (2) which environment we're using for the test (a dedicated staging/pen-test copy vs. production), (3) the cloud provider and account/project details, (4) the application(s) and API endpoints in scope, and (5) the number and roles of test user accounts the firm requested (e.g., unauthenticated, standard user, admin).

Actions to take using my configured credentials:
- Stand up or refresh the designated test environment so it mirrors production closely enough for valid results but contains no real customer data (use synthetic/seed data only).
- Create the requested test accounts with the minimum roles/permissions specified, using unique credentials per account — do not reuse production admin credentials.
- Configure network access so the pen test firm's IP ranges (once provided) can reach the environment, and note any firewall or VPN changes needed.
- Document the environment URL(s), account roles (without secrets), data seeding approach, and teardown plan in a short provisioning memo.
- Flag any in-scope system you cannot isolate from production data so I can decide how to handle it.

Done looks like: the test environment is live and isolated from real customer data, all requested test accounts exist with correct least-privilege roles, network/firewall access is configured or the required change is documented, and I have a provisioning memo summarizing environment details, account roles, and teardown steps — with no credentials or secrets included in your report. Report back with the memo, a list of open questions, and any risks you flagged.

comp_013:n4.prompt:
You are helping me track the testing window for our annual penetration test, which is now underway with the third-party pen test firm we've contracted. Please ask me for: (1) the confirmed testing window start and end dates from the rules-of-engagement, (2) the firm's name and the primary contact (email or portal) for status updates, (3) where our findings tracker lives (e.g., Jira, Linear, a spreadsheet) so you can prep it, and (4) the test environment details already handed off, so you can note them for reference.

Actions to take now: create or update a tracking entry (in our project tracker or a shared doc) recording the testing window dates, the firm and contact, and the environment scope, so everyone knows the test is live. Set up a simple monitoring checklist: when to expect a status check-in from the firm (e.g., midpoint of the window), and the expected date findings or a preliminary report should arrive. Draft a polite status-check email/message template I can send the firm near the midpoint or end of the window to confirm progress, which you should prepare but not send. Also prepare a placeholder findings-triage template (columns: finding, severity, status, owner, due date) so we're ready to load results the moment they arrive.

Important: the actual testing execution — the firm running its tools and manual tests against our environment during this window — remains a human step (in this case, a third-party step) with no interface for you to drive or verify in real time. Do not attempt to check the target environment's logs or systems as if probing on our behalf.

When done, report back: the tracking entry you created/updated, the monitoring checklist and dates, the drafted status-check message (ready for me to send), and the prepared triage template — and confirm you're ready to poll for findings once the window closes.

comp_013:n5.prompt:
You are helping me triage this year's pen test findings into {{vendor}}, our project-management tool, so every finding becomes a tracked issue before our SOC 2 audit. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the pen test firm's findings report (PDF/CSV/export) or its location, (2) my {{vendor}} workspace/project name and API access confirmation using my configured credentials, (3) our severity taxonomy (e.g., Critical/High/Medium/Low) and how it maps to {{vendor}} labels, (4) the engineering lead or team to assign issues to and any due-date policy per severity (e.g., criticals due in 7 days), and (5) any auto-triage or automation rules I want applied (e.g., auto-assign criticals to security lead, auto-tag by finding type).

Once you have this, for each finding in the report: create a tracked issue in {{vendor}} via its documented API, include the finding title, description, affected asset, evidence/reproduction steps, and severity label; assign it to the appropriate owner; set a due date per our severity policy; and link back to the original pen test report line item (in the description or a custom field) for traceability. If {{vendor}} supports AI-assisted triage or automation rules, configure or apply them per my instructions in step 5 so future findings route themselves.

When finished, give me: a summary list of all issues created (issue ID, title, severity, assignee, due date), a link to the {{vendor}} view/filter showing this pen test's findings, and any findings you couldn't file automatically with the reason why. Do not close, resolve, or mark any issue as fixed — that remains a human step for engineers to complete and verify.

comp_013:n6.prompt:
You are helping me remediate the critical and high severity findings from our annual penetration test so we can request a retest and satisfy our SOC 2 auditor. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the pen test findings report or export, (2) access to our issue tracker (e.g., Jira, Linear, GitHub Issues) using my configured credentials, and (3) the repos/systems/environments affected by each finding.

Actions to take:
1. Parse the findings report and extract every finding rated Critical or High, capturing: title, affected asset, description, severity, and recommended fix.
2. For each finding, check the issue tracker for an existing ticket; if none exists, create one with the finding details, severity label, and a due date reflecting urgency (criticals fastest).
3. Where the fix is a clear, low-risk code or configuration change (e.g., patching a dependency, correcting a misconfigured header, tightening an access control), draft the fix as a pull request or config change proposal and link it to the ticket. Do not merge or deploy any change yourself.
4. For findings requiring architectural decisions, third-party coordination, or business judgment, document the recommended remediation approach in the ticket and flag it for a human owner to implement.
5. Update each ticket's status as work progresses (open, in-progress, fixed-pending-verification).
6. Compile a remediation summary listing each critical/high finding, its ticket link, current status, and evidence of the fix (commit link, config diff, or description) for eventual submission to the pen test firm for retest.

Done looks like: every critical and high finding has a tracked ticket, a proposed or completed fix, and a status; low-risk fixes are drafted as ready-to-review PRs but not merged or deployed — that remains a human step. Report back with the full list of findings, their ticket links, fix status, and which items still need a human decision or deployment approval.

comp_013:n7.prompt:
You are helping me close out our annual penetration test by requesting the retest and attestation letter from the pen-test firm we engaged. Before starting, ask me for: (1) the name/contact of the pen-test firm and how we submit requests to them (client portal, ticketing system, or email), (2) the original pen test engagement or ticket ID/reference number, (3) confirmation that all critical and high findings have been remediated (pull status from our findings tracker if I give you access, or ask me to confirm), and (4) any deadline (e.g., SOC 2 audit date) the letter needs to arrive by.

Once you have this, using our configured credentials, log into the firm's client portal or ticketing form (or draft an email if that's their process) and submit a formal request that: references the original engagement ID, states that remediation of all critical/high findings is complete, requests a retest of those specific findings, and requests issuance of a signed attestation letter suitable for our trust center and SOC 2 auditors upon successful retest. Include our desired turnaround date if we have a deadline.

After submission, confirm the request was received (screenshot, confirmation email, or ticket number) and log the submission date, ticket/reference number, and expected response date in a short summary. Note that the firm's actual retest execution and letter issuance remains a human step outside our control, and flag if no acknowledgment arrives within 2 business days so I can follow up.

Report back with: confirmation the request was submitted, the reference/ticket number, expected turnaround, and any follow-up actions needed from me.
